panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Barium swallow in a 73-year-old patient with recurrent diffuse esophageal spasm shows multiple diverticula and hypercontractile segments, supporting DES attribution. b: Endoscopic composite view shows diverticula and hypercontractile rings in the same patient with recurrent diffuse esophageal spasm; these manifestations are not exactly represented in the provided vocabulary, so they are proposed findings.

in_text_mentions: A 73-year-old male patient presented with recurrent dysphagia 6 years after prior peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) for type III achalasia. The recurrent symptoms were mainly attributed to diffuse esophageal spasm coexisting with residual achalasia. Imaging revealed multiple thoracic esophageal diverticula associated with hypercontractile segments ( Fig. 1 ).

panels.rationale: Single-panel fluoroscopic barium swallow of a 91-year-old patient with confirmed diffuse esophageal spasm, showing the classic corkscrew/rosary-bead appearance of the esophagus explicitly attributed to DES in the caption and text. Real patient imaging, no third-party copyright indicated.

premature contractions with a distal latency of less than 4.5 seconds in at least 20% of wet swallows with the assumption of normal lower esophageal sphincter tone [3]. Barium swallow and endoscopy are considered ancillary tests but can provide additional information allowing differentiation of DES from other esophageal disorders [3]. As in this case, the demonstration of classic imaging and clinical presentation along with a thorough history may be sufficient in making the diagnosis of DES. Classic imaging reveals a ‘corkscrew’ appearance of the esophagus, as seen in this patient in Figure 1.

panels.rationale: Single-panel barium esophagogram (fluoroscopic spot image) in a patient with dysphagia whose work-up was positive for diffuse esophageal spasm. The image shows a classic corkscrew/beaded appearance of the distal esophagus with spastic segmental narrowing and uncoordinated contractions, a textbook manifestation of diffuse esophageal spasm; a red arrow annotates the abnormal segment. No third-party copyright, not a diagram or control.

in_text_mentions: physician before arrival to the ER, the patient was started on haloperidol to control her agitated behavior. The patient showed improvement with haloperidol as an outpatient. In the ER, the patient was found to have a sodium level of 121 mEq/L, and urinalysis was positive for infection. Given the evidence of urinary tract infection, the patient was managed with intravenous (IV) antibiotics, and her mental status gradually improved. Because of her dysphagia, the patient was given a speech and swallow evaluation and was recommended an esophagogram, which was positive for diffuse DES (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single-panel barium esophagram from an article titled 'Rare radiological pattern of diffuse esophageal spasm,' showing a dilated proximal esophagus with an abnormal narrowed middle third and abrupt cutoff of barium contrast, consistent with a rare spastic/segmental pattern of diffuse esophageal spasm. The caption describes the arrows and the article title attributes the pattern to diffuse esophageal spasm; the rare/atypical pattern is noted in the title, so typicality is atypical. Patient demographics not stated; no skin visible.

panels.figure_caption: Barium esophagram. Grossly abnormal esophagram with dilated proximal esophagus (white arrow), abnormal appearance of middle one-third (short black arrow) and abrupt cutoff of ingested barium contrast material (short white arrow).
in_text_mentions: phageal strictures and esophageal dilation presented to the emergency department with 12 hours of dysphagia and non-bloody emesis. His symptoms started upon waking and included sharp retrosternal pain during each attempt at swallowing. Dysphagia occurred with both solids and liquid. He denied difficulty initiating swallowing, pain with eating the previous night, halitosis and hematemesis. His vitals and 12-lead electrocardiogram were normal. Despite several attempts at esophageal relaxation using standard methods, he continued having symptoms. At this point an esophagram was obtained (Figure).
